2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable — comparative legal-institutional and policy case study without an empirical participant cohort or panel sample subject to longitudinal attrition.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (uncontrolled) — although historical, hydrological, demographic, and post-conflict contextual factors (e.g., North vs. South water development and colonial dispossession in Australia; Indonesian occupation, infrastructure destruction, poverty, and church opposition in East Timor) are richly described narratively, there is no counterfactual or analytical strategy to separate statutory reform effects from confounding conditions.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate — key statutory, judicial, intergovernmental, and draft legislative instruments in both Australia (Mabo, Native Title Act 1993, 1994 Water Reform Framework, 2004 National Water Initiative paras. 52–54, draft Mataranka Tindal Aquifer Plan) and East Timor (Constitution, 2004 Water Services Decree, 2010 Third Draft National Water Supply Policy, and verbatim provisions of the 2012 Draft Water Resources Law) are situated accurately in institutional context, though several foundational legal sources rely on secondary legal commentary rather than primary legal citations and no systematic legal coding rules are used.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern — the paper reports no primary empirical measurement protocol; claims regarding customary water governance and statutory implementation rely on narrative synthesis of secondary literature, donor reports (e.g., ADB evaluations), unpublished manuscripts, and unverified personal communication.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak — water access, governance recognition, and resource sustainability outcomes are assessed narratively through illustrative examples, secondary estimates (e.g., Indigenous-specific entitlements representing <0.01% of Australian water diversions), and anecdotal compliance observations rather than standardized, systematically collected primary outcome indicators.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern (Can't tell) — no pre-specified study protocol, search strategy, or case/evidence selection criteria are reported, creating risk of selective citation of subnational examples and secondary literature aligned with the authors' normative argument.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern — purposive, undocumented selection of two national jurisdictions and illustrative subnational examples (e.g., Murray-Darling Basin, Katherine/Mataranka, Cape York; Baucau, Oecusse, Dili environs) with no explicit sampling frame or inclusion/exclusion criteria.

domain_ratings.justification: The authors accurately describe major statutory, constitutional, judicial, and policy instruments across both jurisdictions—including Australia's Mabo decision, Native Title Act 1993, 1994 Water Reform Framework, 2004 National Water Initiative (paras. 52–54), and draft Mataranka Tindal Aquifer Plan (DNRETAS, 2011), as well as East Timor's Constitution, 2004 Water Services Decree, 2010 Third Draft National Water Supply Policy, and verbatim text from the unpublished 2012 Draft Water Resources Law (Article 2(a), Article 10(2), and six customary-law sub-articles). Rated 'adequate' rather than 'strong' because several foundational statutes and cases are cited via secondary legal scholarship (e.g., Godden 2005; Bartlett 2004; Gardner et al. 2009) rather than primary statutory/case citations, and the parent article number for the six quoted sub-articles on PDF p. 14 is omitted.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Jackson and Palmer (2012) present a comparative legal-institutional and policy case study examining the interface between statutory water governance reforms ('modernisation') and Indigenous/customary water governance in Australia and East Timor. Because the article has no primary participant recruitment, interview protocol, or systematic literature search—instead combining doctrinal/policy analysis of statutes, intergovernmental agreements, and draft water legislation with published ethnographic and donor-evaluation literature—it is appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework as a structured non-validated judgment (with no numeric score). Methodological strengths lie in its strong jurisdictional specificity (D2) and rich institutional, historical, and cosmological contextualization (D10), supported by adequate legal source accuracy (D1) and exposure characterization (D3), including direct analysis of Australia's Native Title Act 1993, 2004 National Water Initiative, and East Timor's unpublished 2012 Draft Water Resources Law. Conversely, empirical rigour is weak across sampling (D5), case/source selection (D6), outcome definition (D4), measurement transparency (D7), causal identification (D8), treatment of confounding (D9), coding transparency (D12), replication potential (D11), and researcher reflexivity (D13), due to the absence of a documented methodology, reliance on secondary estimates and personal communication, and lack of a counterfactual design.
raw_response.overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Strong institutional contextualization and jurisdictional specificity with adequate legal source accuracy, but weak empirical sampling, measurement, causal identification, coding, and replication transparency
raw_response.study_design_identified: Comparative legal-institutional and policy case study (doctrinal-ethnographic synthesis comparing statutory water reforms and customary water governance in Australia and East Timor)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Design and comparative scope located in Abstract (PDF Page 2) and Introduction (PDF Pages 3–4); funding disclosure in Acknowledgments (PDF Page 2); customary governance context in 'Customary Systems of Water Governance', 'Australia', and 'East Timor' sections (PDF Pages 4–9); legal, policy, and empirical outcome claims in 'Water Governance and Institutional Reform' subsections for Australia and East Timor (PDF Pages 9–16) and 'Discussion'/'Conclusion' (PDF Pages 16–19); sources in 'References' (PDF Pages 20–27). There is no standalone Methods section.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper conducts a comparative institutional, legal-policy, and legal-historical case study of statutory water sector reforms and customary water tenure across Australia and East Timor, analyzing primary and secondary legal/policy texts (including the Native Title Act 1993, 2004 National Water Initiative, 2004 East Timor Water Services Decree, and verbatim provisions of East Timor's 2012 Draft Water Resources Law) alongside published ethnographic research and donor evaluations. It fits none of the six conventional empirical checklists: there is no primary qualitative participant recruitment, interview guide, or qualitative data analysis protocol reported for this study (ruling out CASP Qualitative Checklist, despite a brief acknowledgment of ARC grants supporting Palmer's prior East Timor fieldwork), no systematic review search/screening methodology (ruling out AMSTAR 2), and no quantitative or quasi-experimental dataset (ruling out ROBINS-I, JBI, and RoB 2). Accordingly, per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1–2, the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is the exact matching instrument.
